source.title: DISCOVER: Making Vision Networks Interpretable via Competition and Dissection

record.tranche_reason: The study compares competitive and conventional vision networks using neuron-description and classification measures, a different approach to assessing the architecture-related interpretation claim. It does not directly count polysemantic neurons.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates neuron-label accuracy and description quality, and reports sparse per-example activations. These are indirect measures of interpretability, not a direct measurement of how many neurons respond to unrelated inputs. Table 2's text-embedding cosine scores and qualitative examples are not included as rows because they do not directly measure polysemantic-neuron prevalence. Results for ResNet-50 in Table 3 are cited from prior work and are excluded.
record.test_reason: The paper never measures or names polysemantic neurons. It swaps GELU/ReLU for stochastic LWTA activations in vision networks. It reports classification accuracy, activation sparsity, and CLIP-Dissect description quality (cosine similarity to class names, final-layer label accuracy). None of these is a share of neurons responding to unrelated inputs, so V5 is not tested. Results go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that stochastic LWTA networks keep or improve accuracy with as few as about 4% of neurons active, and that they yield highly interpretable neuron descriptions. The paper never uses the term polysemanticity or measures it.
record.recipe_differences: Uses stochastic LWTA competition in vision networks and CLIP-Dissect-style description matching, rather than the original sources' neuron investigations; tests classification and neuron-label accuracy.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with competitor count, architecture, and probe dataset. The paper also varies concept sets and matching functions for description analyses, but does not report these as polysemanticity measurements.

fits_no_version.finding: Replacing GELU/ReLU with stochastic LWTA yields extreme per-example sparsity (6.25% active for DeiT-T/16 vs 98.56% for GELU on one image). Accuracy stays within about 1.7 points (DeiT-T 72.2 to 70.5–72.5; ResNet-18 52.25 to 49.5–53.9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Competition-based (LWTA) activations make vision-network activations highly sparse per example at small accuracy cost.

fits_no_version.finding: CLIP-Dissect descriptions of the DeiT-T/16 last-layer neurons are slightly closer to class names than DeiT-T/None's (Table 2). Final-layer label accuracy is roughly equal (78.0% vs 78.05–78.3% average, Table 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LWTA activations modestly improve automated neuron-description quality in vision transformers.

record.problems: The study does not directly operationalize or count polysemantic neurons. Neuron-label accuracy measures exact class-label matching, not responses to unrelated inputs. Some comparison results are marked locally reproduced, and the reported neuron-label accuracy table has no DeiT-S/None baseline.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2's CLIP-cosine and mpnet-cosine comparisons, Figures 3 and 5–7, Table 4, and Tables 5–6 are excluded because they report description similarities or qualitative concept lists rather than polysemantic-neuron prevalence. ResNet-50 entries in Table 3 are excluded because the paper attributes those results to prior work.

untested.parts: No test of whether vision neurons respond to unrelated inputs.
No initialization, regularization or noise analysis.
Activation function is changed (LWTA vs GELU/ReLU), but the share of polysemantic neurons is never measured; only accuracy and description-quality proxies are reported.
No re-examination of canonical mixed neurons.
Similarity functions and probe sets are varied, but not as a test of polysemanticity classification.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V5 'tests' and its labels are not justified. Neuron-identification accuracy is computed on the classification layer, where neurons correspond to classes, so it says little about polysemanticity in hidden units. The qualitative claim that GELU neurons give 'irrelevant' concepts (Table 4) is anecdotal, from a single image.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test whether individual vision neurons respond to several unrelated inputs, including the InceptionV1 example.
No language models or token/context responses.
Does not test whether polysemanticity is caused by feature superposition or capacity pressure.
Does not test initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes of polysemanticity without capacity pressure.

Tests competitive versus conventional vision architectures using neuron-label accuracy and classification accuracy, but does not directly measure the share of polysemantic neurons or test modern convnets broadly.
Does not investigate whether canonical mixed-response neurons detect one shared feature or related offshoots.
Although it varies probes and similarity methods for neuron descriptions, it does not test whether polysemantic-neuron counts depend on activation range or explanation scoring.

relation.reason: No polysemantic-neuron test or use. It cites none of the originals and never uses the term. It discusses only neuron specialization and interpretability through description quality, so 'discusses' is the loosest fitting option.

tranche.reason: The paper never measures or names polysemanticity. It reports accuracy, sparsity and CLIP-Dissect description quality (cosine similarity, final-layer label accuracy) for its own LWTA networks. These are a related but different construct, so the paper does not test V5 or any other version. The reader's T2 is not supported.

source_check.notes: All 20 rows match Tables 1 and 3; the DeiT-T/8 and /16 columns are interleaved in the extraction but place unambiguously. The paper's printed Table 3 averages for DeiT-T/16 (78.30%; its cells average 77.25%, below DeiT-T/None's 78.00%) and DeiT-S/2 (78.70%; its cells average 78.53%) don't match the cells. Neuron-label accuracy is for the final layer and does not measure polysemanticity.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: DeiT-T neuron-label accuracy on ImageNet Val and ImageNet Val & Broden; DeiT-T/8 on CIFAR-100 Train; DeiT-S/2 and DeiT-S/12 across their reported probes
reader_labels.reason: Competitive models match or exceed the conventional DeiT-T label-accuracy reference in these settings, and the paper reports strong label accuracy for competitive DeiT-S models (rows T3-06, T3-08 to T3-10, T3-13 to T3-25). These are interpretation-quality proxies, not direct polysemanticity counts.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: DeiT-T neuron-label accuracy on Broden and CIFAR-100 Train; classification accuracy for high-competition models
reader_labels.reason: The competitive DeiT-T models are below the conventional model on Broden and, for DeiT-T/16, CIFAR-100 Train; some high-competition configurations also lower classification accuracy, including ResNet-18/8 on Places365 (rows T1-04, T1-05, T1-09, T1-12, T1-13, T3-07, T3-11, T3-12).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Classification accuracy for the tested competitive vision models
reader_labels.reason: The competitive models retain broadly comparable classification performance, with some exceeding their conventional reference, including DeiT-T/2, DeiT-S/2, and ResNet-18/2 (rows T1-02, T1-07, T1-08, T1-11).
